verse.text: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his slaves what must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his slave John,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master. The Septuagint uses it for Moses and the prophets as God’s own, so here it is a title of honour as well as of belonging. Most English versions soften it to “servants”, which loses the note of ownership a first-century reader would have heard.

verse.text: who testified to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, to all that he saw.
Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of the prophecy, and blessed are those who hear them and keep what is written in it, for the time is near.
verse.note: The Greek has one reader and many hearers. The scene is a gathering in which one person reads the book aloud to the rest, which was the normal way a text reached most people. The blessing falls on that public reader and on the listening community.

verse.text: John, to the seven assemblies in Asia: Grace to you and peace from the one who is and who was and who is coming, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,
verse.note: The word meant a gathering of citizens, and in the Septuagint it is the term for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is well understood, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

note.term: the one who is and who was and who is coming
note.traditional: him who is and who was and who is to come

verse.note: The phrase echoes God’s self-naming in the Greek version of Exodus 3:14, “I am the one who is.” John leaves it grammatically uninflected after a preposition that would normally change its form. This is generally taken as deliberate, treating the phrase as an unchangeable name. The last element is literally “the coming one”, not simply “who will be”.

Many interpreters take this as a symbolic description of the one Spirit of God in its fullness, since it stands between God and Jesus Christ in the greeting. Others take it as seven principal angels who stand before God’s throne. The lower-case plural leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth. To him who loves us and freed us from our sins by his blood—
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “freed” (or “loosed”). Many later manuscripts read “washed”, which in Greek differs by a single letter and sounded almost the same. Modern editions and most modern translations follow the earlier reading.

verse.text: and he made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father—to him be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
Look, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. Yes, amen.

note.term: all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him
note.traditional: all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him

verse.note: The verse weaves together Daniel 7:13 (one coming with the clouds) and Zechariah 12:10 (they look on the one they pierced and mourn). The Greek word for “earth” can also mean “land”, and in Zechariah the mourners are the clans of the land of Israel. Most interpreters think John has widened the scope to all peoples.

verse.text: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “the one who is and who was and who is coming, the Almighty.”
I, John, your brother and partner in the affliction and kingdom and endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek word is an everyday term for distress, pressure or hardship. “Tribulation” is the traditional rendering, but it has become a technical term for an end-time period, which the word does not in itself imply. Some modern versions use “suffering” or “persecution”.

verse.text: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet,
verse.note: This is the earliest known occurrence of the phrase. Most scholars take it to mean the first day of the week, Sunday, as Christian writers of the following generations use it. A minority read it as the prophetic “day of the Lord”, but that is a different expression in Greek.

verse.text: saying, “Write what you see on a scroll and send it to the seven assemblies: to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”
verse.note: The text does not name the owner of the trumpet-like voice. It is attributed here to Jesus because John turns to see the voice and sees the figure of verses 13–18, who repeats the command to write in verse 19. Some interpreters think the first voice belongs to an angel.

verse.text: And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me, and when I turned I saw seven golden lampstands,
and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed in a robe reaching to his feet and with a golden sash wrapped around his chest.

note.term: one like a son of man
note.traditional: one like the Son of Man

verse.note: The wording comes from Daniel 7:13, where “a son of man” is a Semitic way of saying a human being, so the phrase means a figure of human appearance. The Greek has no article, so it is not quite the Gospel title “the Son of Man”, though readers would have made the connection. Translations are divided between the two forms.

verse.text: His head and his hair were white like white wool, like snow, and his eyes were like a flame of fire,
and his feet were like fine bronze when it has been fired in a furnace, and his voice was like the sound of many waters.
verse.note: The Greek word is found only in Revelation (here and 2:18) and in writings that depend on it, so its exact meaning is uncertain. It is clearly a copper alloy of high quality, and guesses include a refined bronze or a brass. The picture of gleaming metal is clear even though the metallurgy is not.

verse.text: He had seven stars in his right hand, and from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in its strength.
When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. And he laid his right hand on me, saying, “Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last,

text.q: and the living one. I was dead, and look, I am alive forever and ever, and I have the keys of death and of Hades.
Write, then, what you have seen, and what is, and what is going to take place after this.

note.term: what you have seen, and what is, and what is going to take place after this
note.traditional: the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this

verse.note: This can be read as three items (the vision just seen, the present situation, the future), and some take it as an outline of the book. It can also be read as two: “what you have seen, both what is and what is going to take place.” The translation keeps the Greek order and lets either reading stand.

text.q: As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies, and the seven lampstands are the seven assemblies.”

verse.note: The Greek word means “messenger” and can be used of a human envoy or of a heavenly being. Everywhere else in Revelation it refers to heavenly beings, so most scholars understand a heavenly representative or guardian of each community. Others take these to be human messengers or leaders of the assemblies.

text.q: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: ‘Thus says the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands:

verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘church’, which nearly all translations keep and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or an institution. ‘Assembly’ is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

The Greek word means ‘messenger’ and can refer to a human envoy as well as a heavenly being. Everywhere else in Revelation it means a heavenly angel, and most scholars take it so here, as a heavenly representative of each community. Others think of a human leader or courier of the assembly, since the messages address the angel as responsible for the community's conduct.

The Greek formula was already old-fashioned in the first century. Readers knew it from the Greek Scriptures as the way the prophets introduced a word from God (‘Thus says the Lord’), and it also had the ring of a royal decree. The slightly archaic English is deliberate.

text.q: I know your works, your labor and your endurance, and that you cannot bear evil people. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them false.
You have endurance, and you have borne up for the sake of my name, and you have not grown weary.
But I have this against you: you have left the love you had at first.
Remember, then, from where you have fallen; turn back and do the works you did at first. If not, I am coming to you, and I will remove your lampstand from its place—unless you turn back.

verse.note: Most translations keep ‘repent’ as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, however, ‘repent’ centres on feeling sorry, while the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. Here the command is paired with resuming former works, which fits that sense.

text.q: But this you do have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.

verse.note: Nothing certain is known about this group beyond what Revelation says. Verses 14–15 associate their teaching with eating food sacrificed to idols and sexual immorality, which suggests they favoured accommodation to the surrounding pagan culture. Later Christian writers connected them with the Nicolaus of Acts 6:5, but that link may be a guess from the name.

text.q: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’
“And to the angel of the assembly in Smyrna write: ‘Thus says the First and the Last, who was dead and came to life:
I know your affliction and your poverty—yet you are rich—and the slander from those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

verse.note: The author, himself a Jew, is writing about a specific local conflict in Smyrna, apparently involving denunciation of the believers (‘slander’). His claim is that these particular opponents have forfeited the name ‘Jews’, which he treats as a title of honour. It is polemic within a first-century dispute over who are the true people of God, not a statement about the Jewish people. The phrase has a long history of misuse against Jews.

text.q: Do not be afraid of anything you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested, and you will have affliction for ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.

verse.note: The Greek word normally denotes a wreath or garland, such as was awarded to victors in athletic contests or worn at festivals, not a king's jewelled diadem. A first-century reader would have pictured a victor's wreath. ‘Of life’ most likely means the wreath that consists in life itself.

text.q: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies. The one who conquers will certainly not be harmed by the second death.’
“And to the angel of the assembly in Pergamum write: ‘Thus says the one who has the sharp two-edged sword:

I know where you live—where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny your faith in me even in the days of Antipas, my witness, my faithful one, who was killed among you, where Satan lives.

verse.note: Pergamum was a leading centre of Roman administration and of emperor worship in the province of Asia, and was also known for its great altar of Zeus and its shrine of the healing god Asclepius. Scholars have proposed each of these as the reference, and it remains uncertain. The imperial cult is the most commonly favoured explanation, since refusal to take part in it could be fatal, as Antipas's death suggests.

text.q: But I have a few things against you: you have there some who hold fast to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel—to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.

verse.note: In Numbers 25 Israelite men are drawn into sexual relations with Moabite women and into the worship of their gods, and Numbers 31:16 blames this on Balaam's advice. Later Jewish tradition developed Balaam into the model of a teacher who leads God's people astray. The name is used here as a label for a teaching current in Pergamum, not as a claim that anyone invoked Balaam.

The verb covers unlawful sexual activity of any kind. In the prophets, and often in Revelation, the same language is a standing metaphor for unfaithfulness to God through idolatry. It is disputed whether literal sexual conduct, participation in pagan worship, or both are meant here and in verses 20–21. The translation keeps the literal wording and leaves the question open.

text.q: So you too have some who in the same way hold fast to the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
So turn back. If not, I am coming to you soon, and I will make war against them with the sword of my mouth.

Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.’

verse.note: The word means a small stone or pebble. Such pebbles were used for voting, including a white one for acquittal in court, and similar tokens could serve as tickets of admission to feasts or as amulets inscribed with a name. Which custom lies behind the image is uncertain, and scholars have not reached agreement.

text.q: “And to the angel of the assembly in Thyatira write: ‘Thus says the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like burnished bronze:

verse.note: The Greek word occurs only here and in Revelation 1:15 and is not found in earlier Greek literature. It clearly denotes some gleaming copper alloy, but exactly which metal is unknown. ‘Burnished bronze’ is a conventional approximation.

text.q: I know your works—your love and faith and service and endurance—and that your last works are greater than the first.
But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, and she teaches and misleads my slaves to commit sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.

verse.note: Most translations have ‘servants’. The Greek word ordinarily meant a slave, someone owned by and wholly at the disposal of a master. In the Greek Scriptures it is also an honourable title for those who belong to God, such as Moses and the prophets. ‘Slaves’ keeps the sense of belonging that a first-century reader would have heard.

Almost certainly a symbolic name, not the woman's own. Jezebel was the queen who promoted the worship of Baal in Israel (1 Kings 16–21; 2 Kings 9). The name casts this influential prophetic teacher in Thyatira in that role. Some manuscripts read ‘your wife Jezebel’, but the shorter reading is generally preferred.

text.q: I gave her time to turn back, but she is not willing to turn back from her sexual immorality.
Look, I am throwing her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they turn back from her works,
and I will kill her children with pestilence. And all the assemblies will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.

verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘kill with death’. In the Greek Scriptures ‘death’ frequently stands for the Hebrew word for plague, and Revelation 6:8 uses it in that sense, so ‘pestilence’ is likely here, especially after the sickbed of verse 22. The alternative is to take the phrase as a Semitic intensive, ‘strike dead’, as a number of translations do. ‘Her children’ probably means her followers.

Literally ‘kidneys and hearts’; the kidneys were regarded as the seat of a person's innermost feelings and motives. The sentence echoes Jeremiah 17:10, where it is God who searches heart and kidneys and repays each according to their deeds. Here the risen Jesus claims that role.

text.q: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching, who have not come to know the deep things of Satan, as they call them, I say: I am laying no other burden on you;
only hold fast to what you have until I come.
And the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end—to that one I will give authority over the nations,

verse.note: The same Greek word is rendered ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in this translation where it means the non-Jewish peoples as distinct from Israel. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so ‘nations’ is used. Verses 26–27 draw on Psalm 2:8–9.

text.q: and that one will shepherd them with an iron rod, as clay pots are smashed to pieces,

verse.note: Most translations have ‘rule’. The verb means to tend a flock and was a common image for a king's government. It comes from the Greek version of Psalm 2:9, where the Hebrew text as traditionally read has ‘break’. Given the smashed pots, some scholars think the sense here is closer to ‘devastate’. ‘Shepherd’ is kept so that the image matches the other places Revelation uses the verb (7:17; 12:5; 19:15).

text.q: just as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give that one the morning star.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies.’

“And to the angel of the assembly in Sardis write: This is what the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars says: I know your works: you have a name for being alive, yet you are dead.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘church’, which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or an institution. ‘Assembly’ is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

Most modern translations render the word ‘reputation’ here, which is its sense. ‘Name’ is kept because the same word runs through the message: the ‘few names’ in Sardis (verse 4, meaning persons) and the name that will not be wiped from the book of life (verse 5). The repetition is deliberate in the Greek.

text.q: Wake up, and strengthen what remains, which was about to die, for I have not found your works complete before my God.

verse.note: Sardis sat on a citadel thought to be impregnable, yet Greek historians record that it was captured more than once by surprise because no adequate watch was kept. Many interpreters think the call to wake up and the warning of a thief’s arrival play on that local memory, though the thief image is also a common early Christian one.

text.q: Remember, then, how you received and heard; keep it, and turn back. If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will certainly not know at what hour I will come upon you.

verse.note: Most translations keep ‘repent’, an established term that readers understand to include a change of life. In current English the word centres on feeling sorry, while the Greek carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. ‘Turn back’ is used for that reason.

text.q: But you have a few names in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy.
The one who conquers will be clothed like this, in white garments, and I will never wipe their name out of the book of life, and I will acknowledge their name before my Father and before his angels.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.
“And to the angel of the assembly in Philadelphia write: This is what the Holy One, the True One, says, the one who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens:

verse.note: The language comes from Isaiah 22:22, where the steward Eliakim is given the key of the house of David, so that what he opens no one shuts and what he shuts no one opens. The key is the authority to admit or exclude from the royal household. Here that authority belongs to the risen Christ.

text.q: I know your works—look, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut—that you have little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.

verse.note: The Greek connective can mean ‘that’ or ‘because’. Taken as ‘that’, the clause states what is known about their works, with the open door as a parenthesis; taken as ‘because’, it gives the reason the door has been opened. The punctuation of the Greek edition followed here favours the first.

text.q: Look, I am giving those from the synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews and are not, but are lying—look, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you.

verse.note: The phrase reflects a local conflict (compare 2:9) between this community and a synagogue in Philadelphia. The writer, himself Jewish, disputes his opponents’ right to the name; it is not a statement about Jews in general. The promise that they will bow at the assembly’s feet reverses Isaiah’s picture of the nations bowing before Israel (Isaiah 60:14; 49:23).

text.q: Because you have kept my word of endurance, I also will keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole inhabited world, to test those who dwell on the earth.

verse.note: The Greek can mean ‘my word about endurance’, that is, Christ’s call to endure, or ‘the word of my endurance’, the message about Christ’s own steadfastness. Most modern translations take it the first way. The rendering here leaves both possible.

text.q: I am coming soon. Hold on to what you have, so that no one takes your wreath.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘crown’. The word normally denotes the wreath awarded to a victor in the games or worn at festivals and honours, and Revelation uses a different word, ‘diadem’, for a ruler’s crown (12:3; 19:12). ‘Wreath’ keeps the image of a prize that can be forfeited. Many scholars are content with ‘crown’, understood as a victor’s crown.

text.q: The one who conquers I will make a pillar in the temple of my God, and they will never go outside again; and I will write on them the name of my God and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from my God, and my own new name.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.
“And to the angel of the assembly in Laodicea write: This is what the Amen says, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation:

note.traditional: the beginning of the creation of God

verse.note: The Greek word can mean ‘beginning’, ‘origin’ or ‘source’, or ‘ruler’. Translations divide among these. ‘Beginning’ is kept because it is the word’s most common sense, and Revelation later calls Christ ‘the beginning and the end’. The phrase is close to the language of Colossians 1:15–18, a letter also meant for Laodicea, where Christ is the one through whom creation came to be. It need not mean that he is the first thing created.

text.q: I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were cold or hot!
So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth.

verse.note: Many interpreters connect the image with local water: nearby Hierapolis had hot springs and Colossae had cold water, while Laodicea’s piped supply arrived tepid. On that reading both hot and cold are useful and the fault is uselessness; the older reading takes cold as hostility and lukewarm as half-heartedness. The verb that follows is the blunt ordinary word for vomiting, often softened to ‘spit’.

text.q: Because you say, ‘I am rich; I have grown rich and need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are the one who is wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked,

I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be exposed, and salve to rub on your eyes so that you may see.

verse.note: The three things offered answer Laodicea’s sources of pride. The city was a wealthy banking centre, was known for its wool cloth, and was associated with a medical school; an eye remedy from the region is mentioned in ancient medical writing. The link between that remedy and Laodicea itself is a reasonable inference, not a certainty.

text.q: All those I love, I reprove and discipline. So be zealous and turn back.
Look, I am standing at the door and knocking. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to them and dine with them, and they with me.
To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.”

verse.text: After this I looked, and there was a door standing open in heaven, and the first voice that I had heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place.” After this,

note.traditional: what must take place after this

verse.note: The closing words of the verse can be attached either to the speech ('what must take place after this') or to the next sentence ('After this, at once I was in the Spirit'). Most English translations take the first option, which echoes Daniel 2 in the Greek Old Testament. This translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used, which begins a new sentence here.

note.term: the first voice that I had heard

verse.note: This points back to the trumpet-like voice of 1:10, where John turns and sees the risen Jesus. On that basis the words are attributed to Jesus here, as most interpreters hold. Some think instead that the voice belongs to an angel who introduces the visions.

verse.text: at once I was in the Spirit; and there was a throne standing in heaven, and on the throne someone was seated.
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could also mean 'in spirit', that is, in a visionary state as opposed to bodily. Most translations take it as a reference to God's Spirit as the source of the prophetic vision, as at 1:10. The two readings are not far apart in practice.

verse.text: The one seated was like jasper stone and carnelian in appearance, and around the throne was a rainbow like emerald in appearance.
Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and on the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.
From the throne came flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder. Seven torches of fire were burning before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God,
verse.note: The word normally means a torch, a blazing brand, not the small oil lamp of a household, for which Greek has a different word. Older English versions and some modern ones have 'lamps'. Several recent translations also use 'torches'.

Many interpreters take this as a symbolic way of speaking of the one Spirit of God in its fullness, seven being the number of completeness, and some translations capitalise accordingly. Others understand seven chief angels who stand before God, an idea known in Jewish writings of the period. The translation leaves 'spirits' in lower case and does not decide the question.

verse.text: and before the throne was something like a sea of glass, like crystal. In the middle of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind.

note.term: In the middle of the throne and around the throne

verse.note: The Greek is hard to picture. It may mean that the creatures stand in the immediate vicinity of the throne, one on each side of it, or that they are in some way part of the throne itself, as the cherubim are in Old Testament throne imagery. The translation keeps the literal wording.

The scene draws on two Old Testament visions: the four living creatures with the faces of a human, lion, ox and eagle in Ezekiel 1, and the six-winged seraphim who cry 'Holy, holy, holy' in Isaiah 6. The word used here is a different one from the 'beast' of later chapters, although the King James Version translated both as 'beast'.

verse.text: The first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature had a face like that of a human, and the fourth living creature was like an eagle in flight.
verse.note: The word can mean a calf, but in the Greek Old Testament it is used widely for bulls and oxen, including for the ox-faced creature of Ezekiel 1:10, which this verse echoes. English versions are divided between 'calf' and 'ox'.

verse.text: The four living creatures, each one of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never rest, saying: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is coming.”
verse.note: The Greek is a present participle, 'the coming one', not a future form of 'to be'. Where one might expect 'who will be', the title says that God is on his way. 'Who is to come' is the usual rendering and is not wrong, but 'who is coming' keeps the sense of approach.

verse.text: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honour and thanks to the one seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,
verse.note: The verbs in verses 9 and 10 are future in Greek ('whenever they will give ... the elders will fall'). Most translators take this as describing repeated, customary action, possibly under Semitic influence, and use the present tense, as here. A minority take it as a real future, pointing forward to the acts of worship narrated later in the book.

verse.text: the twenty-four elders fall down before the one seated on the throne and worship the one who lives forever and ever, and they throw their crowns before the throne, saying:

note.term: throw their crowns before the throne

verse.note: The word covers both a wreath given as a prize or honour and a royal crown; a different word is used later in the book for the diadem of a ruler. Laying one's crown before another was a recognised gesture of submission by subject rulers to an overlord. The elders acknowledge that their honour is derived from the one on the throne.

text.q: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive the glory and the honour and the power, for you created all things, and because of your will they existed and were created.”

verse.note: The Roman writer Suetonius reports that the emperor Domitian was addressed as 'our lord and god'. Many scholars hear a deliberate counter-claim in this acclamation, since Revelation is commonly dated to his reign. The link is plausible but not certain, and the pairing 'Lord' and 'God' is also thoroughly biblical.

The Greek construction expresses the reason or ground for something, not the means: creation exists because God willed it. Most modern versions have 'by your will'; the King James Version has 'for thy pleasure'. The difference is small, but 'because of' is the more exact rendering.

verse.text: And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a scroll, written on the inside and on the back, sealed up with seven seals.

note.term: written on the inside and on the back
note.traditional: a book written within and on the backside

verse.note: The word denotes a papyrus or parchment roll, not a bound book. Scrolls were normally written on the inner side only, so one written on both sides is unusually full; the image recalls the scroll shown to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Legal documents such as wills and deeds were closed with multiple seals, which had to be broken before the contents could be read or put into effect. The Greek says literally 'upon the right hand', so the scroll may be pictured as lying on the open palm.

verse.text: And I saw a strong angel proclaiming in a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”
And no one in heaven or on the earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it.
And I wept bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
But one of the elders said to me, “Do not weep. Look, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

note.term: the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David
note.traditional: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David

verse.note: Both titles are drawn from Scripture and were read as pointing to the Messiah: Judah is called a lion in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:9–10), and Isaiah 11:1, 10 speaks of a shoot from the root of Jesse, David's father. 'Root' here probably means a growth from the root, that is, a descendant of David's line, though some take it to mean David's source.

verse.text: And I saw, in the midst of the throne and the four living creatures and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing, as though slaughtered, with seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.

note.term: in the midst of the throne
note.traditional: in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders

verse.note: The Greek repeats 'in the midst of' in a way that can be read two ways. Either the Lamb stands at the centre, where the throne and living creatures are, surrounded by the elders, or the Lamb stands between the throne with its living creatures on one side and the elders on the other. The rendering keeps the Greek wording and leaves both possibilities open.

The verb is the ordinary word for butchering an animal, used in the Septuagint for sacrificial slaughter and also for violent killing of people. 'Slain' has become a solemn, archaic word that loses this bluntness. Several modern versions also use 'slaughtered'. The same word recurs in verses 9 and 12.

In Jewish Scripture a horn is a standard image of strength and royal power, and seven signifies completeness. The eyes echo Zechariah 4:10, where seven lamps are 'the eyes of the Lord, which range through the whole earth'. Whether 'the seven spirits of God' refers to the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness or to seven angelic beings before the throne is disputed.

verse.text: And he came and took it from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a lyre and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the holy ones.
verse.note: The kithara was a lyre: a handheld instrument with strings stretched from a sound box to a crossbar, and the usual Septuagint word for the instrument of the temple musicians. Most English versions say 'harp', which suggests a different and larger instrument. Some recent translations use 'lyre'.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense here. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

verse.text: And they sang a new song, saying, “You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slaughtered, and with your blood you bought people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation,

note.traditional: redeemed (KJV); ransomed or purchased in many modern versions

verse.note: This is the everyday marketplace word for buying, and it was also used of purchasing slaves. 'Redeemed' and 'ransomed' translate it with words that in English belong to other Greek terms and carry more theological freight than this verb does by itself. The price is named in the same clause: 'with your blood'.

The Greek text translated here has no stated object for 'bought'; 'people' is supplied because English requires one. Many later manuscripts add 'us', and correspondingly read 'made us' and 'we shall reign' in verse 10, which is the basis of the King James wording. Most modern editions judge the shorter reading original, with 'them' in verse 10.

The same Greek word is translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in the New Testament where its plural refers to the non-Jewish peoples. Here, in a fourfold list covering all humanity, it means a nation as an ethnic or political unit. The list echoes similar ones in Daniel (for example Daniel 7:14).

text.q: and you made them a kingdom and priests for our God, and they reign on the earth.”

note.traditional: we shall reign on the earth

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between the present 'they reign' and the future 'they will reign'; the Greek text followed here reads the present, while many translations follow the future. The present may itself look ahead to what is certain. The preposition can also mean 'over the earth'. 'A kingdom and priests' echoes Exodus 19:6, where Israel is called a kingdom of priests.

verse.text: And I looked, and I heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders, and their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,
saying in a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slaughtered to receive power and wealth and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing.”

And every creature in heaven and on the earth and under the earth and on the sea, and all that is in them, I heard saying, “To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever.”
And the four living creatures said, “Amen.” And the elders fell down and worshiped.

note.traditional: fell down and worshipped him that liveth for ever and ever

verse.note: Some late manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'the twenty-four elders' and add 'him who lives forever and ever' as the object of worship. The earliest witnesses lack both expansions, and modern editions omit them. Without the addition, the worship is directed to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, who are named together in verse 13.

verse.text: And I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with a voice of thunder, “Come!”
verse.note: The command is a single word and most naturally summons each horseman, who then appears. Some manuscripts add “and see”, making it an invitation to John; the King James Version follows that reading. The same applies in verses 3, 5 and 7.

verse.text: And I looked, and there was a white horse, and the one seated on it had a bow; and a wreath was given to him, and he went out conquering, and in order to conquer.
verse.note: The word normally means the wreath awarded to a victor or worn at a festival, not a king's crown, for which Revelation uses a different word (diadem). Most translations say “crown”. Here the wreath fits a rider who goes out to conquer. Who this rider is remains disputed: some take him as Christ, others as military conquest, the first of four calamities.

verse.text: And when he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying, “Come!”
And another horse came out, fiery red, and it was given to the one seated on it to take peace from the earth, so that people would slaughter one another; and a great sword was given to him.
And when he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying, “Come!” And I looked, and there was a black horse, and the one seated on it had a pair of scales in his hand.

And I heard what sounded like a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius; and do not damage the oil and the wine!”

note.term: A quart of wheat for a denarius
note.traditional: A measure of wheat for a penny

verse.note: The measure (a choinix, a little over a litre) was roughly one person's daily ration of grain, and a denarius was a typical day's wage for a labourer. These are famine prices, many times the normal rate: a day's work buys only enough wheat for the worker alone, or enough of the cheaper barley for a small family. The command to spare the oil and the wine is variously explained, and its exact point is uncertain.

verse.text: And when he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying, “Come!”

And I looked, and there was a pale green horse, and the one seated on it was named Death, and Hades was following with him. And authority was given to them over a fourth of the earth, to kill with the sword and with famine and with plague, and by the wild beasts of the earth.
verse.note: The word is the ordinary Greek term for the green of plants, and Revelation uses it of grass elsewhere. Applied to people it describes the sickly, greenish pallor of illness or fear, which suits a horse ridden by Death. Most translations say “pale”; some say “pale green” or “ashen”.

The Greek word is the same as the rider's name, Death, and could be rendered “death” here too. In the Septuagint, however, it regularly translates the Hebrew word for pestilence, and the list here echoes the four judgments of Ezekiel 14:21: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. Most modern translations therefore have “plague” or “pestilence”.

verse.text: And when he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slaughtered because of the word of God and because of the testimony they held.
And they cried out with a loud voice, saying, “How long, Master, holy and true, before you pass judgment and avenge our blood on those who live on the earth?”
verse.note: This is not the usual word for “Lord” but the term for the master of a household and owner of slaves, also used of rulers with absolute authority. Many translations render it “Sovereign Lord” or simply “Lord”. “Master” keeps it distinct from the usual word and fits the next verse, where the martyrs' companions are called their fellow slaves.

verse.text: And a white robe was given to each of them, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the number was complete of their fellow slaves and their brothers and sisters who were about to be killed as they themselves had been.
verse.note: The word denotes those who are slaves of the same master, and it answers the address “Master” in the previous verse. Most translations soften it to “fellow servants”. The term was not demeaning in this setting: in the Septuagint, “slave of the Lord” is an honoured title for Moses and the prophets.

note.traditional: until the number should be complete

verse.note: The Greek says only “until they were made complete”; “the number” is supplied, as in most translations, on the understanding that a set number of martyrs must be reached. It could also mean until they had completed their course, and some manuscripts have an active form that favours this.

verse.text: And I watched when he opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth made of hair, and the whole moon became like blood,
and the stars of the sky fell to the earth, as a fig tree drops its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind,
verse.note: The same Greek word means both the visible sky and God's dwelling. Here and in verse 14 the visible sky is in view, with its stars falling and its expanse rolling up, so “sky” is used, as in most modern translations. Older versions have “heaven”.

verse.text: and the sky was split apart like a scroll rolling up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place.
And the kings of the earth and the nobles and the commanders and the rich and the powerful, and every slave and free person, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains;
and they said to the mountains and the rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb,

note.term: Fall on us and hide us

verse.note: The cry echoes Hosea 10:8, and the whole scene of verses 12 to 17 draws on the prophets' pictures of the day of the Lord: the darkened sun and blood-red moon (Joel 2), the sky rolled up like a scroll and stars falling like figs (Isaiah 34:4), and people hiding among the rocks from God's presence (Isaiah 2). The closing question, “who is able to stand?”, likewise recalls Joel 2:11 and Malachi 3:2.

text.q: for the great day of their wrath has come, and who is able to stand?”

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “his wrath”, which the King James Version follows. The reading “their”, referring to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, has strong early support and is adopted by most modern editions; “his” is probably a scribal adjustment to the mention of the Lamb's wrath in the previous verse.

verse.text: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, so that no wind would blow on the earth or on the sea or on any tree.

And I saw another angel coming up from the rising of the sun, holding the seal of the living God, and he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels who had been permitted to harm the earth and the sea,

note.term: the seal of the living God
note.traditional: the seal of the living God

verse.note: A seal was a signet, usually a ring or engraved stone, pressed into wax or clay to mark ownership and guarantee protection. Marking the forehead recalls Ezekiel 9, where those who are marked are spared when judgment falls on Jerusalem. The sealing here marks people as God's property; it does not necessarily promise exemption from suffering.

verse.text: saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we have sealed the slaves of our God on their foreheads.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and the seal on the forehead fits that picture of ownership. Most English versions use “servants,” partly because in the Greek Old Testament “slave of God” was an honorable title for Moses, David and the prophets. Both associations would have been heard by a first-century reader; “slaves” is kept here because “servant” now suggests a paid employee free to leave.

verse.text: And I heard the number of those who were sealed, a hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:
verse.note: The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand, and most interpreters take it as symbolic of completeness. Whether this group is the same as the uncountable crowd of verse 9 is disputed. On one view John hears the number and then sees the crowd, two pictures of one people. On the other, the 144,000 are a distinct group, such as Jewish believers. The Greek does not settle it.

verse.text: from the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Gad, twelve thousand;
verse.note: This list matches no Old Testament list of the tribes. Judah, the tribe of the Messiah, comes first instead of the firstborn Reuben. Dan is missing, and both Joseph and his son Manasseh are counted while Ephraim is not named. The reasons for the omission of Dan are debated; an association of that tribe with idolatry is the explanation most often proposed.

verse.text: from the tribe of Asher, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Naphtali, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Manasseh, twelve thousand;
from the tribe of Simeon, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Levi, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand;
from the tribe of Zebulun, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Joseph, twelve thousand; from the tribe of Benjamin, twelve thousand sealed.

After these things I looked, and there was a great crowd that no one could count, from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.
verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is often translated “Gentiles,” meaning the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation, where the scope is all the peoples of the world, it is rendered “nation” or “nations.”

Palm branches were carried in celebrations of victory and at festivals, especially the Feast of Tabernacles, and the crowd waves them when Jesus enters Jerusalem in John 12:13. Together with the white robes they mark the scene as a victory celebration.

verse.text: And they cry out with a loud voice, saying, “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”
verse.note: The Greek is a shout without a verb: “The salvation to our God.” In the Greek Old Testament the word often means deliverance or victory won in battle, and some translators render it “Victory” here. The traditional “salvation” is kept, but the sense is that the rescue is God's achievement and the credit is his.

verse.text: And all the angels were standing around the throne and the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,
saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might belong to our God forever and ever. Amen.”
Then one of the elders spoke up and said to me, “These who are clothed in the white robes, who are they, and where have they come from?”
And I said to him, “My lord, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great affliction; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verse.note: The word means pressure, distress or oppression and is the ordinary term for the sufferings of God's people; “the great affliction” echoes Daniel 12:1. “Tribulation” has become a technical term in some modern end-time schemes, which a first-century reader would not have heard in it. Whether a single final crisis or the whole course of persecution is meant is disputed.

note.traditional: they which came out / the ones who have come out

verse.note: The Greek uses a present participle, which may picture people still arriving as John watches. It may equally be a timeless description, “those who come out,” and many versions translate it as a completed action. The rendering here keeps the present form.

text.q: For this reason they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple, and the one who sits on the throne will spread his tent over them.

note.term: will spread his tent over them

verse.note: The verb means to pitch a tent or encamp, and with the preposition “over” it pictures God's tent stretched above the worshippers as shelter. It recalls the tabernacle, the tent of God's presence in the wilderness. Many versions paraphrase as “dwell among them” or “shelter them with his presence.”

text.q: They will hunger no more and thirst no more; the sun will never beat down on them, nor any scorching heat,

note.term: They will hunger no more and thirst no more
note.traditional: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more

verse.note: Verses 16 and 17 weave together promises from Isaiah without quoting them formally. No hunger, thirst or scorching sun, and guidance to springs of water, come from Isaiah 49:10; God wiping away tears comes from Isaiah 25:8. In Isaiah it is God who shepherds and guides; here that role is given to the Lamb.

text.q: because the Lamb at the center of the throne will shepherd them and guide them to springs of the waters of life, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

verse.text: And when he opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verse.note: The Greek gives no subject. The one opening the seals is the Lamb, who began opening them in chapter 6; some translations supply “the Lamb” here for clarity.

The text does not explain the silence, and interpreters differ. Some take it as the hush of awe before God acts in judgment, a motif found in the prophets; others connect it with the incense offering that follows, as though heaven falls quiet so that the prayers of God's people may be heard.

verse.text: And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.

note.term: the seven angels who stand before God

verse.note: The definite article points to a group the readers were expected to know. Jewish tradition spoke of seven angels who attend in God's immediate presence (for example Tobit 12:15), later often called archangels.

verse.text: And another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a golden censer, and much incense was given to him to offer with the prayers of all the holy ones on the golden altar that is before the throne.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people.”

The Greek is a bare dative, here and in verse 4. It may mean the incense is offered together with the prayers, or on behalf of the prayers, or even that the incense represents the prayers themselves (compare 5:8). “With” is the most common rendering and leaves the relationship open.

verse.text: And the smoke of the incense went up with the prayers of the holy ones from the angel’s hand before God.
Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it to the earth, and there came peals of thunder and rumblings and flashes of lightning and an earthquake.
verse.note: The Greek word means both “voice” and “sound.” Older versions have “voices,” but most modern translations render “rumblings.” The cluster of thunder, sounds, lightning and earthquake recalls God's appearance at Sinai in Exodus 19 and recurs in Revelation at climactic moments.

verse.text: And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound them.

The first sounded his trumpet, and there came hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was thrown to the earth; and a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up.

note.term: hail and fire mixed with blood

verse.note: The trumpet judgments echo the plagues on Egypt in Exodus: hail with fire, water turned to blood, and darkness. A reader steeped in the Scriptures would have recognised the pattern of God judging an oppressor before delivering his people.

verse.text: The second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea; and a third of the sea became blood,
and a third of the creatures in the sea, those that had life, died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
The third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star fell from the sky, burning like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.
verse.note: The same Greek word means both “heaven” and “sky.” It is rendered “heaven” in verse 1, where God's dwelling is in view, and “sky” here, where a star falls. Some translations keep “heaven” here; the Greek does not distinguish the two.

verse.text: The name of the star is Wormwood. And a third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters, because they had been made bitter.
verse.note: Wormwood is an intensely bitter plant. In the Hebrew Scriptures it is an image of bitter suffering and divine judgment (for example Jeremiah 9:15), and the name here signals what the star does to the waters. The plant itself is not normally deadly; the image is symbolic.

verse.text: The fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them would be darkened, and the day would not shine for a third of it, and the night likewise.

And I looked, and I heard an eagle flying high overhead, saying with a loud voice, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the remaining trumpet blasts of the three angels who are about to sound!”
verse.note: The earliest and best manuscripts read “eagle”; many later manuscripts read “angel,” which is why the King James Version has “an angel.” The Greek word can also mean a vulture, a bird associated with impending death, and some interpreters prefer that sense here.

The Greek word is an astronomical term for the highest point of the sky, where the sun stands at noon. “Midheaven” or “the midst of heaven” is the traditional rendering, but it can suggest a region halfway up or a middle tier of heaven. The point is that the eagle is at the zenith, visible and audible to all.

verse.text: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star that had fallen from the sky to the earth, and the key to the shaft of the abyss was given to him.
verse.note: In Jewish writing of the period, stars often stand for heavenly beings, and this one acts as a person: it receives a key and opens the shaft. The Greek pronoun can be read as "it" or "him"; "him" is used because the star acts as an agent. Whether this figure is a fallen, evil being or simply an angel sent down from heaven is disputed.

The older English rendering "the bottomless pit" merges two Greek words: one for a well or shaft, and "abyss." In the Greek Old Testament "abyss" is the primeval deep, and by the first century it also named the underground prison of hostile spirits. The picture is of a locked shaft leading down into that realm; several modern translations render it similarly.

verse.text: He opened the shaft of the abyss, and smoke rose out of the shaft like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the shaft.
And out of the smoke locusts came onto the earth, and power was given to them like the power that the scorpions of the earth have.
They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only the people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
They were not allowed to kill them, but only to torment them for five months; and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings a person.
In those days people will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, and death flees from them.
In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. On their heads was something like crowns that looked like gold, and their faces were like human faces;
verse.note: The Greek word normally means a wreath of the kind awarded to victors or worn at festivals, though it could also be made of gold and worn by rulers. Revelation uses a different word for the royal diadem. The hedged wording ("something like... that looked like gold") is the author's own: the vision is described by comparison throughout.

verse.text: they had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like lions’ teeth;
they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots with many horses charging into battle.
They have tails like scorpions, with stingers, and in their tails is their power to harm people for five months.
They have as king over them the angel of the abyss; his name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he has the name Apollyon.
verse.note: Abaddon is a Hebrew word meaning "destruction," used in the Old Testament as a name for the realm of the dead alongside Sheol. Here it is the name of a person, and the Greek equivalent given, Apollyon, means "Destroyer." Some scholars also hear an echo of the god Apollo's name, but this is uncertain.

verse.text: The first woe has passed; look, two woes are still coming after this.
And the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a single voice from the horns of the golden altar that is before God,
verse.note: Many manuscripts read "the four horns of the golden altar," and a number of translations follow them. Other early witnesses lack "four," and the SBLGNT text translated here omits it. The meaning is not affected, since an Israelite altar had a horn at each of its four corners.

verse.text: saying to the sixth angel, the one who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”
verse.note: In the Old Testament the Euphrates was the far boundary of the promised land and the direction from which invading empires such as Assyria and Babylon came. In the first century it was also the eastern frontier of the Roman empire, beyond which lay the Parthians, renowned for their cavalry. A first-century reader would have heard an invasion from the east in this image.

verse.text: So the four angels were released, who had been prepared for that hour and day and month and year, to kill a third of humanity.
The number of the cavalry troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.

note.term: twice ten thousand times ten thousand

verse.note: The Greek is literally "two myriads of myriads," a myriad being ten thousand, which comes to two hundred million; some translations give the figure outright. The phrasing echoes Old Testament language for countless heavenly hosts (as in Daniel 7:10) and was probably heard as an overwhelming number rather than a precise count.

verse.text: And this is how I saw the horses in the vision, and those seated on them: they had breastplates of fiery red, dark blue, and sulfur yellow. The heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and out of their mouths come fire and smoke and sulfur.
verse.note: The Greek word names the color of the hyacinth, a dark blue or violet, and is used in the Greek Old Testament for blue-dyed cloth. The three colors of the breastplates match the fire, smoke and sulfur that come from the horses' mouths, the dark blue answering to the smoke. The Greek could mean that the horses as well as the riders wear the breastplates.

verse.text: By these three plagues a third of humanity was killed, by the fire and the smoke and the sulfur coming out of their mouths.
For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails; for their tails are like snakes, having heads, and with them they do harm.

And the rest of humanity, those who were not killed by these plagues, did not turn back from the works of their hands so as to stop worshiping the demons and the idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk;
verse.note: The traditional rendering is "repent," which most translations keep as an established term understood to include a change of life. In current English, however, "repent" centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. Here the sense is that the survivors did not abandon their idols and their crimes.

verse.text: and they did not turn back from their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verse.note: The Greek word means drugs or potions, and by extension the charms and spells of magical practice; it could also mean poisons, which would suit its place next to "murders." Most translations take it as magic in general, and that is followed here. Some manuscripts have a closely related noun that names the practice of sorcery more directly.

verse.text: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with the rainbow over his head; his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire,
verse.note: The Greek word usually means 'foot' but can take in the leg as well, and the comparison to pillars suggests legs here. The same word is rendered 'foot' in verse 2, where the angel plants one on the sea and one on the land. Older versions have 'feet' in both places; most recent ones have 'legs' here.

verse.text: and he held in his hand a little scroll that lay open. He set his right foot on the sea and his left on the land,
verse.note: The word is a diminutive of the ordinary term for a scroll, which is what a 'book' was at this period. Verse 8 calls the same object simply 'the scroll', so the diminutive may carry little weight. Whether this scroll is related to the sealed scroll of chapter 5 is debated.

verse.text: and he cried out with a loud voice, as a lion roars. And when he cried out, the seven thunders spoke with their own voices.
When the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders said, and do not write it down.”
Then the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven

note.term: raised his right hand to heaven

verse.note: Raising the hand toward heaven was the gesture of a solemn oath. The scene closely echoes Daniel 12:7, where an angelic figure raises his hands to heaven and swears by the one who lives forever about how long it will be until the end.

verse.text: and swore by the one who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, and the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it: “There will be no more delay,

note.term: There will be no more delay
note.traditional: there should be time no longer

verse.note: The Greek says literally 'time will be no longer'. Older versions took this as the end of time itself. Almost all modern scholars and translations read it as 'no more time will pass', that is, no further delay, which fits the 'but' that follows and the echo of Daniel 12, where the question is how long until the end.

text.q: but in the days of the sound of the seventh angel, when he is about to blow his trumpet, the mystery of God will be accomplished, as he announced the good news to his own slaves the prophets.”

verse.note: The Greek verb is a past tense ('was accomplished'), used here of a future event that is treated as certain. English needs a future to make sense of the sentence. The verb means to bring to completion or fulfilment.

The phrase is a stock Old Testament expression, and English Bibles traditionally say 'servants'. The Greek word was the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way; applied to the prophets it expresses total belonging to God and was a title of honour. Many scholars accept 'slave' as the more accurate rendering, though 'servant' remains the majority choice in translations.

verse.text: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke with me again and said, “Go, take the scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”
So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, “Take it and eat it up. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”

note.term: Take it and eat it up

verse.note: The scene reworks Ezekiel 2:8–3:3, where the prophet is given a scroll to eat and finds it sweet as honey in his mouth. Eating the scroll stands for taking in the message the prophet must then deliver. The bitterness that follows here is usually understood as the painful content of that message, though the text does not explain it.

verse.text: I took the little scroll from the angel’s hand and ate it up, and in my mouth it was sweet as honey; but when I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter.
Then they said to me, “You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”
verse.note: The verb is plural, with no stated subject. It may be an indefinite plural meaning simply 'I was told', or it may refer to the heavenly voice and the angel together. Some manuscripts have the singular 'he says', which older versions followed.

The preposition can mean 'about', 'against' or 'in the presence of'. Most modern translations choose 'about'; older ones have 'before', and some scholars argue for 'against', since the prophecies that follow are largely of judgment.

The Greek word rendered 'nations' here is the same word translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. In lists like this one in Revelation, the peoples of the whole world are in view, so 'nations' is used.

verse.text: And a reed like a staff was given to me, with the words, “Get up and measure the sanctuary of God and the altar and those who worship in it.

note.traditional: and the angel stood, saying (KJV); and I was told

verse.note: The Greek has only the participle 'saying', with no stated speaker. 'My two witnesses' in verse 3 suggests God or Christ is speaking, or an angel on their behalf; some later manuscripts supply 'the angel stood', which the KJV follows. The speech is taken here to end at verse 3, since verse 4 refers to the Lord in the third person, but the Greek does not mark where it closes.

Most translations have 'temple'. The Greek word used here is the one for the sanctuary building itself, the dwelling place of the deity, as distinct from the wider temple precinct with its courts. That distinction matters in this passage, where the outer courtyard lies outside what is measured. The same word is used for God's sanctuary in heaven in verse 19.

text.q: But leave out the courtyard outside the sanctuary and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

verse.note: One Greek word means both 'nations' and, in Jewish usage, 'Gentiles' (the non-Jewish peoples). Older translations have 'Gentiles' here, and the trampling of the holy city by foreigners supports that nuance. 'Nations' is used because Revelation consistently has the peoples of the whole world in view; the same word appears in verses 9 and 18.

Forty-two months, the 1,260 days of verse 3, and three and a half years are the same span. It echoes the 'time, times and half a time' of Daniel (7:25; 12:7), a limited period in which God's people are oppressed. The three and a half days of verses 9 and 11 play on the same figure.

text.q: And I will grant it to my two witnesses to prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

verse.text: These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.

note.term: the two olive trees and the two lampstands

verse.note: The image comes from Zechariah 4, where a lampstand is flanked by two olive trees identified as the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. These are usually understood as the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua. In Revelation 1:20 lampstands stand for churches.

verse.text: And if anyone wants to harm them, fire comes out of their mouths and consumes their enemies; and if anyone should want to harm them, this is how that person must be killed.

These have the authority to shut the sky, so that no rain falls during the days of their prophesying, and they have authority over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.
verse.note: The powers described recall Elijah, who announced a drought and called down fire on his enemies (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 1), and Moses, who turned water to blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7–11). Whether the two witnesses are meant to be particular individuals, such as Moses and Elijah returned, or a symbol of the witnessing church is disputed.

verse.text: And when they finish their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war on them and conquer them and kill them.
And their corpses lie on the main street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified.
verse.note: 'Where their Lord also was crucified' points to Jerusalem, and many interpreters take it so. Elsewhere in Revelation, however, 'the great city' is Babylon, generally understood as Rome. Others therefore read it as a symbol of the world city hostile to God wherever it is found. The text does not settle the question.

Most modern translations have 'symbolically' or 'figuratively'. The word is literally 'spiritually', and elsewhere in the New Testament it means in a manner belonging to or given by the Spirit. The sense is probably that the names Sodom and Egypt express the city's true character as the Spirit discloses it, which is more than a figure of speech, so the older rendering is kept.

verse.text: And some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations look at their corpses for three and a half days, and they do not allow their corpses to be placed in a tomb.
And those who live on the earth rejoice over them and celebrate, and they will send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who live on the earth.
And after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell on those who were watching them.

note.traditional: the Spirit of life (KJV); a breath of life

verse.note: The Greek word means both 'breath' and 'spirit', so 'a spirit of life' or 'the Spirit of life' is also possible. The wording echoes Ezekiel 37, where breath enters the slain and they stand on their feet, so 'breath' is chosen. A first-century reader would likely have heard both senses.

verse.text: And they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up into heaven in the cloud, and their enemies watched them.

And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell, and seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest became terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.
The second woe has passed. Look, the third woe is coming soon.

And the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever.”
And the twenty-four elders who sit before God on their thrones fell on their faces and worshiped God,
saying, “We give you thanks, Lord God, the Almighty, the one who is and who was, because you have taken your great power and begun to reign.

note.term: the one who is and who was
note.traditional: which art, and wast, and art to come (KJV)

verse.note: Some later manuscripts add 'and who is to come', matching the fuller formula in 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8; the KJV follows them. The earliest and best witnesses lack the phrase here. The shorter form fits the context: God's coming is no longer future, because he has begun to reign.

text.q: The nations were angry, and your anger has come, and the time for the dead to be judged, and to give the reward to your slaves the prophets and to the holy ones and to those who fear your name, the small and the great, and to destroy those who destroy the earth.”

verse.note: Most translations have 'servants'. The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone owned by a master, and that is how a first-century reader heard it. 'My slaves the prophets' is a standing phrase in the Greek Old Testament, where it is a title of honor for those wholly at God's disposal.

Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'. 'Saints' now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel.

note.traditional: thy wrath is come; your wrath has come

verse.note: Most translations have 'the nations were angry' (or 'raged') and then 'your wrath'. The Greek uses a verb and a noun from the same root, setting the anger of the nations against the anger of God, so one English word is used for both. The verse closes with a similar play, 'destroy those who destroy'.

verse.text: And God's sanctuary in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his sanctuary; and there were flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder and an earthquake and heavy hail.
And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and on her head a crown of twelve stars.
She was pregnant, and she was crying out in labor pains, in agony to give birth.
And another sign appeared in heaven—and look, a great fiery-red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a huge serpent or sea monster, not the winged, fire-breathing creature of later European legend. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for Leviathan and for the chaos monsters that stand for powers hostile to God, such as Pharaoh's Egypt. Verse 9 identifies this one with the serpent of Genesis.

This is a different word from the 'crown' of verse 1. That word denotes a wreath of victory or honor; this one is the band worn by a king as the emblem of sovereignty. The dragon's seven diadems are a claim to royal rule.

verse.text: His tail dragged a third of the stars of the sky and hurled them to the earth. And the dragon stood in front of the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she gave birth he might devour her child.
verse.note: This is the same Greek word translated 'heaven' elsewhere in the chapter; it covers both the visible sky and the dwelling of God. 'Sky' is used here because the stars are in view. In a vision like this the two senses are not sharply separated.

verse.text: She gave birth to a son, a male child, who is going to shepherd all the nations with an iron rod. And her child was snatched away to God and to his throne.
verse.note: The verb means to tend a flock and, by extension, to govern. The phrase echoes Psalm 2:9 in its Greek form, which has 'shepherd them with an iron rod' where the Hebrew as traditionally read has 'break them'. Most translations render 'rule'; 'shepherd' keeps the image, in which the rod is the herdsman's club. Some scholars think the context of the psalm gives the verb a harsher sense here, closer to 'crush'.

The Greek word is the one translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in the New Testament where it means the non-Jewish peoples. It is rendered 'nations' here, as usual in Revelation, because the scope is every people of the world.

verse.text: And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that there she might be nourished for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.

note.term: one thousand two hundred and sixty days

verse.note: This equals forty-two months of thirty days, or three and a half years. It is the same period as the 'time and times and half a time' of verse 14, a phrase taken from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, where it marks a limited period of persecution of God's people.

verse.text: And war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels made war on the dragon. The dragon and his angels made war,
but he did not prevail, and no place was found for them in heaven any longer.

And the great dragon was hurled down—the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan, the one who leads the whole inhabited world astray—he was hurled to the earth, and his angels were hurled down with him.
