verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for a slanderer or false accuser. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate the Hebrew 'satan', an adversary or accuser, as in the opening of Job. The original audience would have heard that meaning, and verse 10 picks it up by calling him 'the accuser'.

verse.text: And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, because the accuser of our brothers and sisters has been hurled down, the one who accuses them before our God day and night.

text.q: And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives even to the point of death.

note.traditional: by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony

verse.note: Most translations have 'by', which presents the blood and the testimony as the means of victory. The Greek construction (this preposition with the accusative case) normally gives the ground or reason: 'because of', 'on account of'. The difference is slight, and some scholars think the construction here does shade toward means.

text.q: Therefore rejoice, you heavens and you who dwell in them! Woe to the earth and the sea, because the Devil has come down to you in great fury, knowing that he has only a short time.”

verse.text: And when the dragon saw that he had been hurled to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.
verse.note: The verb means both to chase and to persecute, and older translations have 'persecuted'. The narrative of flight in verses 14 to 16 favors 'pursued'. A reader in a persecuted church would have heard both senses.

verse.text: But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle, so that she might fly into the wilderness, to her place, where she is nourished for a time and times and half a time, away from the presence of the serpent.

note.term: the two wings of the great eagle

verse.note: The image recalls the exodus, where God tells Israel, 'I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself' (Exodus 19:4; compare Deuteronomy 32:11). The woman's flight into the wilderness, where she is fed, follows the same pattern of rescue and provision.

verse.text: And the serpent hurled water like a river from his mouth after the woman, to have her carried off by the river.
But the earth came to the woman’s help: the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had hurled from his mouth.
And the dragon was enraged at the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, those who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus.
verse.note: The word is literally 'seed', and it echoes Genesis 3:15, where God puts enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between his seed and hers. Having called the dragon 'the ancient serpent' in verse 9, the chapter shows that enmity carried on against the woman's other children.

The Greek can mean the testimony Jesus himself bore, which his followers hold on to, or their testimony about Jesus. Scholars are divided, and the phrase recurs elsewhere in Revelation with the same ambiguity. The translation leaves it open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: And he stood on the sand of the sea.

note.traditional: I stood upon the sand of the sea

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'he stood', meaning the dragon, who takes up a position on the shore before the beast rises from the sea. Many later manuscripts read 'I stood', which makes John the subject; the two forms differ by one letter. Older translations follow the later reading and attach the sentence to 13:1, and some modern editions number it 13:1 as well.

verse.text: Then I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, and on its horns ten diadems, and on its heads blasphemous names.

note.term: a beast rising out of the sea
note.traditional: a beast rising out of the sea

verse.note: The description draws on Daniel 7, where four beasts come up out of the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard and a ten-horned monster, standing for successive empires. Here their features are combined into a single creature. Most interpreters take it as a picture of imperial power, with Rome as its first-century form.

verse.text: The beast I saw was like a leopard, its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And the dragon gave it his power and his throne and great authority.
One of its heads looked as if it had been slaughtered to death, yet its fatal wound was healed. The whole earth followed the beast in amazement,

note.traditional: wounded to death / seemed to have a mortal wound

verse.note: Most translations smooth this to ‘wounded’ or ‘a mortal wound’. The Greek uses the same verb, in the same form, that describes the Lamb ‘as though slaughtered’ in 5:6 and again in verse 8 of this chapter. The beast is presented as a counterfeit of the Lamb, with its own death and recovery, and keeping one English word lets the reader see that.

verse.text: and they worshipped the dragon because he had given authority to the beast, and they worshipped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?”
It was given a mouth speaking great boasts and blasphemies, and it was given authority to act for forty-two months.
verse.note: The passive ‘was given’ (rendered ‘was allowed’ before a verb) recurs through the chapter, in verses 5, 7, 14 and 15. It is usually understood as a reverent way of saying that the beasts act only within limits God permits. The dragon’s grant of power in verse 2 is stated separately and in the active voice.

Forty-two months is three and a half years, the same span as the 1,260 days and the ‘time, times and half a time’ elsewhere in Revelation (11:2–3; 12:6, 14). The figure comes from Daniel (7:25; 12:7), where it marks a limited period of oppression of God’s people.

verse.text: It opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his dwelling, those who dwell in heaven.
It was allowed to make war on the holy ones and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation.
verse.note: ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God’s people’.

The Greek word here is the same one this translation renders ‘Gentiles’ where the non-Jewish peoples are meant. In Revelation’s fourfold formula ‘tribe and people and language and nation’ the scope is the whole world, so ‘nation’ is used.

verse.text: And all who live on the earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered from the foundation of the world.

note.term: from the foundation of the world
note.traditional: the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world

verse.note: The translation follows the Greek word order, in which the phrase sits next to ‘slaughtered’. It can equally be attached to ‘written’: ‘whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered’. Revelation 17:8 has that sense without ambiguity, and many scholars and translations read this verse the same way. Opinion is divided.

verse.text: If anyone has an ear, let them hear.
If anyone is for captivity, into captivity they go; if anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they are to be killed. This calls for the endurance and the faith of the holy ones.

note.term: by the sword they are to be killed
note.traditional: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword

verse.note: The manuscripts vary considerably here. Many read ‘if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed’, a warning of retribution. SBLGNT follows the reading of Codex Alexandrinus, in which both halves speak of a fate to be accepted, echoing Jeremiah 15:2. That reading is harder Greek, and most textual critics think it gave rise to the others.
The Greek word covers both trust and faithfulness. Paired here with ‘endurance’ under persecution, it may well mean loyalty that holds firm, and some translations render it ‘faithfulness’.

verse.text: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon.
It exercises all the authority of the first beast before its eyes, and it makes the earth and those who live on it worship the first beast, whose fatal wound was healed.
It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to the earth before people’s eyes.

It leads astray those who live on the earth because of the signs it was allowed to perform before the eyes of the beast, telling those who live on the earth to make an image for the beast, which has the wound of the sword and yet lived.
It was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast could even speak and could cause all who would not worship the image of the beast to be killed.
It causes everyone, the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the slaves, to be given a mark on their right hand or on their forehead,
verse.note: The word was used for a stamped or engraved impression, such as a brand, the impress on a coin, or an official seal on a document. In Revelation it is the counterpart to the seal placed on the foreheads of God’s servants (7:3; 14:1). Whether a literal mark is envisaged or a symbol of allegiance is disputed.

verse.text: so that no one can buy or sell except the one who has the mark: the name of the beast or the number of its name.
This calls for wisdom. Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a person; and its number is six hundred and sixty-six.
verse.note: The Greek can mean the number of a particular human being, which fits a name to be worked out, or ‘a human number’, meaning one reckoned in the ordinary human way (compare ‘a human measure’ in 21:17). The translation takes the first sense, which is the more common view.

A few early witnesses read 616, a variant already known in the second century, but 666 is much better attested. Greek and Hebrew letters doubled as numerals, so a name could be ‘calculated’ by adding up its letters. The most widely held solution is ‘Nero Caesar’ written in Hebrew letters, which gives 666, or 616 in a spelling closer to the Latin form. The identification is not certain.

verse.text: Then I looked, and there was the Lamb, standing on Mount Zion, and with him a hundred and forty-four thousand who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.
And I heard a sound from heaven like the sound of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder, and the sound I heard was like harpists playing on their harps.

And they sing what seems a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. No one could learn the song except the hundred and forty-four thousand, who have been bought from the earth.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary marketplace word for buying, the same one used just before (13:17) of those who cannot buy or sell without the beast’s mark. Most English versions render it “redeemed” here and in verse 4, which is theologically apt but hides both the plainness of the word and the echo. The image is of people purchased to belong to God.

verse.text: These are the ones who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were bought from among humankind as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb,
verse.note: The word is normally used of women, and its application to this company is striking. It can be read literally, of celibacy, or figuratively, of fidelity to God: the prophets regularly picture idolatry as sexual unfaithfulness, and this chapter goes on to speak of Babylon’s prostitution. Most interpreters take it figuratively, some seeing an allusion to the abstinence required of Israel’s soldiers on campaign, but the point is disputed.

verse.text: and no lie was found in their mouth; they are blameless.
Then I saw another angel flying high overhead, with eternal good news to announce to those who live on the earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people,
verse.note: The Greek word meant good news or a public announcement of it, and here it has no article and is paired with its own verb, “to announce good news.” Most translations use “gospel.” Interpreters differ on whether this is the Christian message as such or a specific summons, given in verse 7, to fear God as his judgment arrives.

The same Greek word, in the plural, is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in this translation when it means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation’s lists of peoples, and in “all the nations” in verse 8, the scope is the whole world, so “nation” is used.

verse.text: saying in a loud voice, “Fear God and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment has come; and worship the one who made heaven and earth and sea and springs of water.”
Then another angel, a second, followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the fury of her prostitution.”
verse.note: The cry echoes Isaiah 21:9. Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in the sixth century BC; most scholars think the name here stands for Rome, which did the same in AD 70. Some read it more broadly as any imperial power set against God.

note.term: the wine of the fury of her prostitution
note.traditional: the wine of the wrath of her fornication

verse.note: The Greek word can mean either passion or anger. Many translations use “passion” here and “wrath” in verses 10 and 19; others think the wine is one that brings God’s wrath on those who drink it. “Fury” is used in all three places so that the echo is audible: those who drink Babylon’s wine will drink God’s. “Prostitution” replaces the traditional “fornication” because Babylon is later pictured as a prostitute, an image the prophets use for idolatry and corrupting alliances.

verse.text: Then another angel, a third, followed them, saying in a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on their forehead or on their hand,

text.q: that person too will drink the wine of God’s fury, poured undiluted into the cup of his wrath, and will be tormented with fire and sulfur before holy angels and before the Lamb.

verse.note: The Greek says literally “mixed unmixed.” Wine was normally mixed with water before drinking, and the verb for mixing had come to be used for preparing or pouring a drink. Undiluted wine is wine at full strength: the image is of judgment with nothing to soften it.

text.q: And the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever, and they have no rest day or night, those who worship the beast and its image, and anyone who receives the mark of its name.”

verse.text: Here is the endurance of the holy ones, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus.
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek is literally “the faith of Jesus,” and “their” is supplied. Most translations understand it as faith in Jesus, as here. It could also mean faithfulness to Jesus, or the faithfulness that Jesus himself showed, to which they hold fast.

verse.text: And I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “so that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.”
Then I looked, and there was a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand.

note.term: one like a son of man
note.traditional: one like unto the Son of man

verse.note: The phrase comes from Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man,” a Semitic way of saying a human figure, comes with the clouds of heaven; Revelation 1:13 uses it of the risen Christ. Most interpreters identify the figure here as Christ. A minority think an angel is meant, since “another angel” follows and gives him the command to reap.

verse.text: And another angel came out of the temple, crying out in a loud voice to the one seated on the cloud, “Put in your sickle and reap, for the hour to reap has come, because the harvest of the earth is fully ripe.”
So the one seated on the cloud swung his sickle over the earth, and the earth was reaped.
Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle.

And another angel came from the altar, the one who has authority over the fire, and he called in a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, “Put in your sharp sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe.”
So the angel swung his sickle into the earth and gathered the vintage of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of God’s fury.
And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as the horses’ bridles, for sixteen hundred stadia.

note.traditional: a thousand and six hundred furlongs

verse.note: A stadion was about 185 metres, so the distance is roughly 300 kilometres, or about 185 miles. Many interpreters think the figure is symbolic, since it is the square of four multiplied by the square of ten, but its exact significance is uncertain.

verse.text: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvelous: seven angels with seven plagues, the last ones, because with them the fury of God is completed.
verse.note: Most translations use "wrath" both for this word and for a second Greek word, orgē. Revelation uses the two side by side (for example 16:19), and this word is the more heated term, denoting an outburst of anger. "Fury" keeps the two apart; the difference in meaning is one of intensity, not of kind.

verse.text: And I saw what looked like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing on the sea of glass, holding lyres of God.

note.term: standing on the sea of glass
note.traditional: standing on (or beside) the sea of glass

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mean either "on" or "at, beside". Some translations have the victors standing on the shore of the sea, as Israel stood beside the Red Sea when Moses sang; others have them standing on its glassy surface. Either reading is possible.

The kithara was a hand-held stringed instrument of the lyre family, played with a plectrum. It was not a harp in the modern sense. Most English versions keep "harps" from long tradition. "Lyres of God" probably means lyres given by God or used in his service.

verse.text: And they sing the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: “Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God, the Almighty! Righteous and true are your ways, King of the ages!
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone who belongs to a master. Most translations soften it to "servant". In the Greek Old Testament, "slave of the Lord" is also a title of honor for Moses and the prophets, marking them as wholly at God's disposal, and that sense is in view here.

The reference is to the song Moses and Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 15), and perhaps also to Moses' final song in Deuteronomy 32. The words that follow do not quote either. They are woven from phrases in the Psalms, Deuteronomy and Jeremiah.

The manuscripts are divided between "King of the ages" and "King of the nations"; a few late copies have "King of saints", the reading behind the King James Version. The edition translated here prints "ages", but many scholars and translations prefer "nations", which echoes Jeremiah 10:7. The evidence is closely balanced.

text.q: Who will not fear, Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. For all the nations will come and worship before you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”

verse.note: The Greek word is the same one rendered "Gentiles" elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. Here the scope is all the peoples of the world, so "nations" is used. The line echoes Psalm 86:9.

The word can mean a righteous deed, or a decree or judicial sentence. Some translations therefore have "your judgments have been revealed", meaning God's verdicts on the world. "Righteous acts" keeps the link with "righteous" in the previous line, which is from the same Greek word-family.

verse.text: After this I looked, and the temple of the tent of testimony in heaven was opened,
verse.note: This is the Greek Old Testament's name for the tent sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness, which housed the tablets of the covenant, called the "testimony". John sees its heavenly counterpart. The phrase probably means "the temple, that is, the tent of testimony".

verse.text: and out of the temple came the seven angels who had the seven plagues, clothed in clean, bright linen and with golden sashes wrapped around their chests.
verse.note: Some important early manuscripts read "stone" (lithon) instead of "linen" (linon), a difference of one letter. That reading would have the angels clothed in pure bright stone. Most editors and translations regard "stone" as a copying error and read "linen".

verse.text: Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the fury of God, who lives forever and ever.
And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.
Then I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels, “Go and pour out the seven bowls of the fury of God onto the earth.”

note.term: a loud voice from the temple

verse.note: The speaker is not identified. Because the previous verse (15:8) says no one could enter the temple until the plagues were finished, many interpreters take the voice to be God's own, as also the voice from the throne in verse 17. The text leaves it unnamed, and the translation does the same.

Most translations render this word 'wrath' here. Verse 19 uses it side by side with a second Greek word for anger (orgē), and translations then need two English words. This translation uses 'fury' for the first and 'wrath' for the second throughout the chapter, so the reader can see that the bowls of verse 1 and the cup of verse 19 share the same term.

verse.text: So the first went and poured out his bowl onto the earth, and a foul and malignant sore came upon the people who had the mark of the beast and who worshipped its image.
The second poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a corpse, and every living creature died, everything in the sea.
The third poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
And I heard the angel of the waters saying, “You are just, you who are and who were, the Holy One, because you have given these judgments,
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice'. Here and in verse 7 the subject is God's judging, so 'just' is used. Older versions have 'righteous' in both places.

The King James Version reads 'which art, and wast, and shalt be', following an edition of the Greek text that rested here on a scholarly conjecture, not on manuscripts. The manuscripts read 'the Holy One', and all modern editions follow them. The Greek word is different from the one behind 'holy ones' in verse 6. It describes one who is devout or faithful, and in the Septuagint is used of God as well as of his loyal people.

text.q: for they poured out the blood of holy ones and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it.”

verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God. Many translations keep 'saints', and others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

verse.text: And I heard the altar saying, “Yes, Lord God, the Almighty, true and just are your judgments.”
The fourth poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire.
People were scorched with a fierce heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has authority over these plagues, and they did not turn back to give him glory.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repent', which in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

verse.text: The fifth poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues from the pain,
and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and they did not turn back from their deeds.
The sixth poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, so that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun.
verse.note: The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, and beyond it lay the Parthian empire, Rome's most feared rival. For a first-century reader, a dried-up Euphrates meant the border standing open to invasion from the east. The image also recalls the drying of the Red Sea and the Jordan, and the prophets' oracles about the fall of Babylon, which stood on this river.

verse.text: And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet.
For they are spirits of demons performing signs, which go out to the kings of the whole inhabited world to gather them for the battle of the great day of God the Almighty.

text.q: “Look, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes on, so that he will not walk about naked and have people see his shame.”

note.term: “Look, I am coming like a thief.

verse.note: The narrative is interrupted by a voice speaking in the first person. No speaker is named, but the words match what the risen Jesus says to the churches earlier in the book (3:3 on coming like a thief, 3:18 on clothing and the shame of nakedness), and the saying is generally taken as his. The description of the kings being gathered resumes in verse 16.

verse.text: And they gathered them to the place that is called in Hebrew Harmagedon.
verse.note: The familiar spelling 'Armageddon' comes from a different manuscript tradition. It has also become an English word for a world-ending catastrophe, whereas here it is a place name. The form printed follows the Greek text being translated. It is usually explained as Hebrew for 'mountain of Megiddo', a city on a plain where famous Old Testament battles were fought. No mountain of that name is known, and the derivation is disputed.

verse.text: The seventh poured out his bowl on the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, “It is done!”

And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings and peals of thunder, and there was a great earthquake, such as there had never been since people came to be on the earth, so mighty an earthquake, so great.
The great city split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. And Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.
verse.note: It is disputed which city is meant. Many take it to be Babylon, named in the next sentence and called 'the great city' later in the book. Others take it to be Jerusalem, which is called 'the great city' at 11:8 and would then be distinguished from 'the cities of the nations'. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

verse.text: Every island fled, and no mountains were to be found.
And huge hailstones, each weighing about a talent, came down from the sky on people, and people blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, for that plague was exceedingly great.

note.traditional: about a hundred pounds; the weight of a talent

verse.note: A talent was the largest common unit of weight. Its value varied with place and period, but estimates generally fall somewhere between about 25 and 40 kilograms (roughly 60 to 90 pounds). The point is hailstones of impossible size, far beyond anything in the Exodus plague of hail that the scene recalls.

verse.text: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying, “Come, I will show you the judgment on the great prostitute who sits on many waters,

note.term: the great prostitute who sits on many waters

verse.note: The Hebrew prophets pictured great cities as prostitutes: Tyre in Isaiah 23, Nineveh in Nahum 3, and Jerusalem itself in Ezekiel 16 and 23. The phrase ‘on many waters’ echoes Jeremiah 51:13, addressed to historical Babylon with its river and canals. A reader steeped in the Greek Old Testament would have heard a city being described before the angel says so in verse 18.

text.q: with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality, and those who live on the earth became drunk on the wine of her prostitution.”

verse.note: The Greek noun covers unlawful sexual activity in general and is traditionally rendered ‘fornication’ or ‘sexual immorality’. It shares a root with the word for ‘prostitute’ and is here the conduct of a figure so named, so it is rendered ‘prostitution’; the verb translated ‘committed sexual immorality’ is from the same root. In the prophets this imagery stands for idolatry and corrupting alliances, and most interpreters read it that way here.

verse.text: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns.
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could mean either ‘in the Spirit’ (carried by God’s Spirit) or ‘in spirit’ (in a visionary state rather than bodily). The same phrase marks the major vision scenes of the book (1:10, 4:2, 21:10). Most translations capitalize, as here, but the two senses are not far apart.

verse.text: The woman was clothed in purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her prostitution,
and on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: “Babylon the Great, the mother of prostitutes and of the abominations of the earth.”
verse.note: The word can be read as part of the inscribed name (‘Mystery, Babylon the Great’, as in the King James Version) or as a comment that the name has a hidden meaning. Most modern translations take the second view, as here, since the angel goes on to explain ‘the mystery of the woman’ in verse 7. In the usage of the period the word means a secret now being disclosed, not an unsolvable puzzle.

verse.text: And I saw the woman drunk on the blood of the holy ones and on the blood of the witnesses of Jesus. When I saw her, I was utterly amazed.
verse.note: Traditionally ‘saints’, which now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God’s people’.

The Greek word means ‘witness’, one who testifies; the English word ‘martyr’ derives from it. Many translations use ‘martyrs’ here because these witnesses have been killed. Whether the word had already acquired the technical sense ‘one who dies for the faith’ when Revelation was written is disputed, so the ordinary meaning is kept.

verse.text: And the angel said to me, “Why are you amazed? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, the one with the seven heads and the ten horns.

text.q: The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss, and it goes to destruction. And those who live on the earth, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will be amazed when they see that the beast was, and is not, and will come.

verse.note: The description parodies the title given to God earlier in the book, ‘the one who is and who was and who is coming’ (1:4, 1:8, 4:8). The beast imitates this, but its middle term is ‘is not’ and its end is destruction. Many scholars also see an allusion to the widespread rumour that Nero would return after his death, though this is not certain.

text.q: This calls for a mind that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. They are also seven kings:

verse.note: The Greek word covers both mountains and hills. Rome was known throughout the ancient world as the city on seven hills, and most scholars think first readers would have recognized Rome at once, with ‘Babylon’ as its cipher. Some interpreters instead identify the city as Jerusalem or as a symbol of oppressive worldly power in general.

text.q: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must remain for a little while.

note.term: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come

verse.note: The identity of the seven kings is disputed. Some match them to particular Roman emperors, though there is no agreement on where to begin counting or whom to include; others take them as successive empires. Others again read seven as a symbolic number for the full span of hostile rule. The text does not settle the question.

text.q: As for the beast that was and is not, it is itself an eighth, and it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

verse.note: The Greek is literally ‘is of the seven’. It may mean that the eighth is one of the seven returning, or that it comes from the seven and shares their character without being one of them. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

text.q: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received kingship, but they receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘kingdom’ in verses 12 and 17 and ‘reigns’ or ‘has dominion’ in verse 18. Here the word means not a territory but royal rule itself, the status and power of a king, and one English word is used for all three occurrences. This also keeps the play in verse 18 between ‘kingship’ and ‘kings’.

text.q: These have one purpose, and they give their power and authority to the beast.
These will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”

verse.text: And he said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples and crowds and nations and languages.
verse.note: The same Greek word is rendered ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in this translation where it refers to the non-Jewish peoples as a group. Here it stands in a fourfold list describing the population of the whole world, a formula that recurs throughout Revelation, so ‘nations’ is used.

text.q: And the ten horns that you saw, and the beast, these will hate the prostitute and will make her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her up with fire,
for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, and to act with one purpose and give their kingship to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.
And the woman that you saw is the great city that holds kingship over the kings of the earth.”

verse.text: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven. He had great authority, and the earth was lit up by his glory.

And he cried out with a mighty voice, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place of demons, a prison for every unclean spirit, a prison for every unclean bird, and a prison for every unclean and hated beast,

note.term: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!

verse.note: The cry echoes Isaiah 21:9. The whole chapter is built from the prophets' dirges over ancient Babylon and over the trading city of Tyre (Isaiah 13, 23 and 47; Jeremiah 50–51; Ezekiel 26–28). A first-century reader steeped in the Septuagint would have heard those oracles being reapplied to the great city of the preceding chapter.

The Greek word ordinarily means a prison or guard-post, and it means prison elsewhere in Revelation (2:10; 20:7). Most translations soften it to ‘haunt’ because the background in Isaiah pictures ruins inhabited by wild creatures. The ordinary sense is kept here: the fallen city is where unclean things are confined, though ‘lair’ or ‘haunt’ remains a common scholarly reading.

note.term: a prison for every unclean and hated beast
note.traditional: a cage of every unclean and hateful bird

verse.note: The manuscripts differ over how many items stand in this list. Some have only spirits and birds, others spirits and beasts, others all three; the shorter forms probably arose when a copyist's eye skipped between the repeated phrases. The edition translated here prints all three, while some critical editions bracket the clause about beasts as doubtful.

text.q: because all the nations have fallen by the wine of the passion of her prostitution, and the kings of the earth prostituted themselves with her, and the merchants of the earth grew rich from the power of her luxury.”

verse.note: The Greek words for ‘have fallen’ and ‘have drunk’ differ by a single letter, and the manuscripts are divided. ‘Have fallen’ has strong early support and is the reading of the edition translated here. Many editors and most translations prefer ‘have drunk’ because it suits the image of wine and matches 14:8 and 17:2.

The Greek word is the same one translated ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in the New Testament. It means a people or nation, and in the plural often means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation's phrase ‘all the nations’ the scope is the whole world, so ‘nations’ is used.

The word can mean either intense passion or anger, and elsewhere in Revelation it usually refers to God's wrath. Here it may describe the intoxicating passion of Babylon's prostitution, or the wrath that her prostitution brings down on those who drink. Translations are divided; the first reading is followed.

The noun and its verb (‘prostituted themselves’) share a root with the word for the prostitute who personifies the city in chapter 17, and the rendering keeps that link visible. The image comes from the prophets, who described a city's corrupting alliances and trade as prostitution (for example Isaiah 23:17 of Tyre). Most translations use ‘fornication’, ‘sexual immorality’ or ‘adulteries’; the sense is figurative in any case.

verse.text: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, so that you do not share in her sins and do not receive any of her plagues,
verse.note: The voice is not identified. ‘My people’ suggests God or Christ, and the call echoes Jeremiah 51:45, yet the voice goes on to speak of God in the third person (verses 5 and 8), so it may be an angel speaking on God's behalf. It is also uncertain where the speech ends: it is closed here at verse 8, but some interpreters run it through verse 20.

text.q: for her sins have piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her crimes.
Pay her back as she herself has paid, and pay her double for what she has done; in the cup she mixed, mix her a double measure.
As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her that much torment and mourning. For in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen; I am no widow, and mourning I will never see.’
For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire, for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”

verse.text: And the kings of the earth, who prostituted themselves with her and lived in luxury with her, will weep and beat their breasts over her when they see the smoke of her burning,
standing far off for fear of her torment, saying, “Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon the mighty city! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”
And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargo any more,

cargo of gold and silver and precious stones and pearls, and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet, and every kind of citron wood and every article of ivory and every article of the most precious wood and bronze and iron and marble,
and cinnamon and spice and incense and perfumed oil and frankincense, and wine and olive oil and fine flour and wheat, and cattle and sheep, and horses and carriages and slaves—and human lives.
verse.note: The word rendered ‘slaves’ is literally ‘bodies’, the ordinary commercial term for slaves in the Greek of the period. The closing phrase, literally ‘souls of people’, is the Septuagint's expression for human beings traded as merchandise (Ezekiel 27:13). Placed at the end of the cargo list, it may simply restate ‘slaves’ or may add a pointed comment that these goods are human lives.

verse.text: The ripe fruit your soul craved has gone from you, and all that was rich and splendid is lost to you, and never again will they be found.

note.term: The ripe fruit your soul craved has gone from you

verse.note: The Greek turns without warning to address Babylon directly, and no speaker is named. Some translations put the verse in the merchants' mouths, and others treat it as part of the heavenly voice that began in verse 4. It is left here, like verse 20, as an unattributed address, without quotation marks.

verse.text: The merchants of these things, who grew rich from her, will stand far off for fear of her torment, weeping and mourning,
saying, “Woe, woe, the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls!
For in a single hour such great riches have been laid waste.” And every helmsman and everyone who sails for any port, and sailors and all who make their living from the sea, stood far off
and cried out as they watched the smoke of her burning, saying, “What city is like the great city?”

And they threw dust on their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning, saying, “Woe, woe, the great city, where all who had ships at sea grew rich from her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.”
Rejoice over her, heaven, and you holy ones and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her.
verse.note: ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God's people’.

note.term: given judgment for you against her
note.traditional: God hath avenged you on her

verse.note: The Greek is compressed, literally ‘God has judged your judgment from her’. It may mean that God has upheld their case against her, or that God has exacted from her the sentence she once passed on them. The rendering follows the first reading, which is the more common, but the second is well supported.

verse.text: Then a mighty angel picked up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So, with violence, will Babylon the great city be thrown down, and she will never be found again.

text.q: The sound of harpists and musicians and pipers and trumpeters will never be heard in you again; no craftsman of any craft will ever be found in you again; the sound of a mill will never be heard in you again;

the light of a lamp will never shine in you again; the voice of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again. For your merchants were the magnates of the earth, for all the nations were led astray by your sorcery,
and in her was found the blood of prophets and holy ones, and of all who have been slaughtered on the earth.”

verse.text: After this I heard what sounded like the loud voice of a great crowd in heaven, saying, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God,
verse.note: A Hebrew phrase meaning ‘praise Yah’ (a short form of God's name), carried over untranslated into Greek. Readers knew it from the Greek Psalms, where it stands as a heading or refrain. Its four occurrences in this chapter (verses 1, 3, 4 and 6) are the only ones in the New Testament.

text.q: for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her prostitution, and he has avenged on her the blood of his slaves.”

verse.note: This is the city called Babylon, whose fall fills chapters 17–18. The Hebrew prophets used prostitution as an image for a city's idolatry and its corrupting commerce, and the charge here is of that kind rather than literal. Older versions have ‘whore’ or ‘harlot’ and ‘fornication’; ‘prostitute’ and ‘prostitution’ keep the Greek's play on two words from one root.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and it is the same word translated ‘slave’ in verse 18. In the Greek Old Testament ‘slaves of God’ is an honourable title for Moses and the prophets, marking them as belonging wholly to God. Most translations soften it to ‘servants’, which in modern English suggests a paid employee.

verse.text: And a second time they said, “Hallelujah! Her smoke goes up forever and ever.”
And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshipped God, who sits on the throne, saying, “Amen! Hallelujah!”
And a voice came from the throne, saying, “Praise our God, all you his slaves, and you who fear him, the small and the great.”
And I heard what sounded like the voice of a great crowd, like the sound of many waters and like the sound of mighty thunders, saying, “Hallelujah! For the Lord God, the Almighty, has begun to reign.
verse.note: The Greek verb is in a past tense that can mark the start of a state (‘has become king’, ‘has taken up his reign’) or simply state the fact (‘reigns’). The same form opens several Psalms in the Greek Old Testament, where it is usually translated ‘the Lord reigns’. The rendering here takes it of God's rule now openly established with Babylon's fall; many translations have ‘reigns’.

text.q: Let us rejoice and be glad, and we will give him the glory, for the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready,

note.term: we will give him the glory
note.traditional: let us give him the glory

verse.note: The manuscripts divide between ‘we will give’ and ‘let us give’, which differ in Greek by a few letters. The edition translated here prints the future; most English translations follow the other reading, which matches the two preceding verbs.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for ‘woman’ or ‘wife’, not the word for ‘bride’ used in 21:2. A betrothed woman was already called a man's wife before the wedding took place, so the word fits a wedding that has only now arrived. Many modern translations have ‘bride’.

verse.text: and it was granted to her to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and pure.” For the fine linen is the righteous acts of the holy ones.
verse.note: The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God's people’ or ‘his holy people’.

verse.text: And he said to me, “Write: ‘Blessed are those who have been invited to the wedding banquet of the Lamb.’” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.”

note.term: the wedding banquet of the Lamb
note.traditional: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verse.note: The Greek word is the main meal of the day and, on formal occasions, a banquet; ‘supper’ now suggests a light evening meal. The same word returns in verse 17 for ‘the great banquet of God’, a grim counterpart in which birds feed on the fallen. That scene draws on Ezekiel 39:17–20.

verse.text: And I fell down before his feet to worship him. But he said to me, “Don’t do that! I am a fellow slave with you and with your brothers and sisters who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”
verse.note: The Greek can mean testimony about Jesus or the testimony that Jesus himself gave, and scholars are divided. The English ‘of’ is kept because it leaves both open. The closing sentence is correspondingly open: either witness to Jesus is the heart of prophecy, or what Jesus testified is what the prophetic Spirit speaks.

verse.text: And I saw heaven standing open, and look, a white horse! Its rider is called Faithful and True, and with justice he judges and makes war.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Elsewhere this translation uses ‘righteousness’, but here the subject is judging and waging war, so fair judgment is meant. Most translations keep ‘in righteousness’; the phrase echoes the Psalms' picture of God judging the world.

verse.text: His eyes are a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems. He has a name written that no one knows except himself,
and he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and his name is called the Logos of God.
verse.note: Manuscripts vary between ‘dipped’ and several forms of ‘sprinkled’. The picture draws on Isaiah 63:1–3, where God comes with garments stained from treading the winepress. Interpreters disagree whether the blood is that of his enemies, his own, or that of the martyrs; the text does not say.

Nearly all translations have ‘the Word of God’. This translation keeps the Greek title in the four verses where it names a person, because ‘the Word of God’ now commonly means the Bible. Most scholars find the main background in the Hebrew Bible's ‘word of the Lord’ and in Wisdom traditions, which ‘Word’ reflects and ‘Logos’ does not. Wisdom of Solomon 18:15–16 pictures God's word leaping from heaven as a warrior with a sharp sword.

verse.text: And the armies in heaven were following him on white horses, dressed in fine linen, white and pure.

From his mouth comes a sharp sword, so that with it he may strike down the nations, and he himself will shepherd them with an iron rod; and he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the furious wrath of God the Almighty.
verse.note: The verb means to tend a flock and is often used in the Greek Old Testament for a king's rule. The line quotes Psalm 2:9 in its Greek form, which has ‘shepherd’ where the traditional Hebrew text reads ‘break’. Most translations have ‘rule’; ‘shepherd’ keeps the image of a herdsman's iron-tipped club, which here is a weapon and not a gentle guide.

verse.text: And on his robe and on his thigh he has a name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.
And I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying to all the birds flying high overhead, “Come, gather for the great banquet of God,

text.q: to eat the flesh of kings and the flesh of commanders and the flesh of the mighty, the flesh of horses and of their riders, and the flesh of all, free and slave, small and great.”

verse.text: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to make war against the rider on the horse and against his army.

And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who had performed the signs in its presence, by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshipped its image. The two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.
And the rest were killed by the sword of the rider on the horse, the sword that came out of his mouth, and all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh.
Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding the key to the abyss and a great chain in his hand.
verse.note: The KJV and several modern versions render this 'bottomless pit'. In the Septuagint the word means the primeval deep, and in Jewish writings of the period it had become a name for the underworld prison of rebellious spirits. 'Abyss' keeps that association without adding the image of a pit, which the Greek word does not itself supply.

verse.text: He seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years,
verse.note: This is the only passage in the New Testament that speaks of a thousand-year reign. Interpreters have long disagreed over whether it is a future period on earth after Christ's return, a symbolic picture of the present age between his resurrection and return, or something else. The translation does not decide between these readings.

verse.text: and threw him into the abyss, and shut and sealed it over him, so that he would no longer lead the nations astray until the thousand years were completed. After that he must be released for a short time.
verse.note: Most translations have 'deceive'. The verb means to cause to wander or go off course, and in the Septuagint it is the usual word for leading people away into idolatry. 'Lead astray' keeps that sense of being drawn off the right path and not simply told something false.

The Greek word here is the same one translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in the New Testament. It means peoples or nations, and in the plural often the non-Jewish peoples specifically. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so 'nations' is used.

verse.text: Then I saw thrones, and they sat on them, and judgment was given to them. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received the mark on their forehead or on their hand. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verse.note: The Greek can mean either that those seated were given authority to judge or that a verdict was given in their favor. The scene echoes Daniel 7:22, where the wording is similarly open. The text does not say who is seated on the thrones; the rendering leaves both questions as the Greek leaves them.

The verb is a simple past of 'live', which can mean 'they lived' or 'they came to life'. Most modern translations take it as 'came to life', as the same form is used of Christ's resurrection in 2:8. Whether this is a bodily resurrection or a spiritual one is disputed and is tied to how the thousand years are understood.

verse.text: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection.

Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection! Over these the second death has no authority, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verse.note: Most translations say the second death has no 'power' over them. The Greek word denotes the right or jurisdiction to act, not raw force, so 'authority' is the closer equivalent: the second death has no claim on these people.

verse.text: And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison,
and he will go out to lead astray the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for the war; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verse.note: The names come from Ezekiel 38–39, where Gog, of the land of Magog, leads a vast army against a restored Israel and is destroyed by God. By the first century the pair had become a byword in Jewish tradition for the hostile nations of the final battle. Here they stand for the nations of the whole earth, not for one identifiable people.

verse.text: They went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the holy ones and the beloved city. And fire came down from heaven and consumed them.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of God's people as those set apart for him, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

Many later manuscripts read 'from God out of heaven', and the KJV follows them. The shorter reading translated here has early support and is adopted by most modern critical editions. The longer form was probably influenced by the similar wording in 21:2 and 21:10.

verse.text: And the devil, who was leading them astray, was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet also are, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
Then I saw a great white throne and the one seated on it. From his presence earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them.

And I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works.
verse.note: A first-century reader would have pictured scrolls, not bound volumes. The image of heavenly records opened at the judgment comes from Daniel 7:10. The 'book of life' recalls a city's register of citizens, an image already used in the Old Testament (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1).

verse.text: The sea gave up the dead that were in it, and Death and Hades gave up the dead that were in them, and they were judged, each one according to their works.
Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire.
And anyone not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.
Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.
verse.note: In the Scriptures and in Revelation itself the sea stands for chaos and threat; the beast rises from it (13:1) and it holds the dead (20:13). Its absence signals the removal of everything hostile to God's order, not a remark about geography.

verse.text: And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband.
And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Look, the dwelling of God is with humanity, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his peoples, and God himself will be with them,
verse.note: The Greek word means a tent and is the Septuagint's term for the tabernacle, the tent-sanctuary where God was present with Israel in the wilderness. The verb “dwell” that follows comes from the same root, and the English keeps that echo. The promise takes up Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27.

note.term: they will be his peoples, and God himself will be with them
note.traditional: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between the plural “peoples” and the singular “people”; the plural, followed here, widens the old covenant formula for Israel to many peoples. Many manuscripts also add “as their God” (or “and be their God”) at the end of the verse; the Greek text translated here does not include it.

text.q: and he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more; neither mourning nor crying nor pain will be any more. The first things have passed away.”

verse.text: And the one seated on the throne said, “Look, I am making all things new.” And he said, “Write this, for these words are faithful and true.”
And he said to me, “They have come to pass. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the one who is thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life, free of charge.
verse.note: The Greek verb is plural, literally “they have happened,” and most likely refers to the words just declared faithful and true, or to the “all things” being made new. Most translations give the singular “It is done,” matching the similar cry at 16:17, where the Greek is in fact singular.

text.q: The one who conquers will inherit these things, and I will be his God and he will be my son.

note.term: I will be his God and he will be my son

verse.note: This echoes God's promise about David's heir in 2 Samuel 7:14, “I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me.” The royal promise is here extended to everyone who conquers, male or female. The singular “son” is kept so that the allusion stays audible.

text.q: But as for the cowardly and faithless and detestable, and murderers and the sexually immoral and sorcerers and idolaters and all liars, their share is in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”

verse.note: The word can mean either “unbelieving” or “unfaithful, untrustworthy.” Following “cowardly,” and in a book addressed to churches under pressure to give way, it probably points to failure of loyalty rather than simply to outsiders who do not believe. Many translations nevertheless have “unbelieving.”

verse.text: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues came and spoke with me, saying, “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.”
And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could also be read “in spirit,” describing a visionary state rather than naming God's Spirit. The same phrase occurs at 1:10, 4:2 and 17:3. The language recalls Ezekiel 40:2, where the prophet is taken in visions to a very high mountain to see the restored city.

verse.text: having the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal.
It had a great, high wall; it had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names inscribed on them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel:
on the east three gates, and on the north three gates, and on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.
And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
The one who was speaking with me had a golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and its wall.
The city is laid out as a square, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with the rod: twelve thousand stadia. Its length and width and height are equal.
verse.note: A stadion was roughly 185 metres, so the figure comes to about 2,200 kilometres (some 1,400 miles) in each dimension. The number is kept as written because it is symbolic, twelve times a thousand, matching the twelves that run through the chapter. A city of equal length, width and height recalls the cube-shaped inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20).

verse.text: He also measured its wall: one hundred forty-four cubits by human measure, which is also the angel’s.

note.term: one hundred forty-four cubits by human measure, which is also the angel’s

verse.note: A cubit was about 45 centimetres, so the wall measures roughly 65 metres; the number is twelve times twelve. The text does not say whether this is the wall's height or its thickness, and interpreters are divided. The closing phrase seems to mean that the angel is using ordinary human units, though its exact sense is disputed.

verse.text: The material of its wall was jasper, and the city was pure gold, like pure glass.
The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every kind of precious stone. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald,
verse.note: Ancient gem names do not map neatly onto modern mineralogy, and the identification of several stones in this list is uncertain. The stone called “sapphire,” for example, was probably lapis lazuli, and “jasper” covered a wider range of stones than it does today. The list resembles the stones on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17–20), though the two do not correspond exactly.

verse.text: the fifth sardonyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst.
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; each one of the gates was made from a single pearl. And the main street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
verse.note: The word means a broad street and can also denote an open square or plaza. It is singular here, and could be meant collectively for the city's streets in general.

verse.text: I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God, the Almighty, is its temple, and the Lamb.
And the city has no need of the sun or of the moon to shine on it, for the glory of God has illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb.
The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it.
verse.note: This is the same Greek word that elsewhere in the New Testament is translated “Gentiles,” meaning the non-Jewish peoples. Here, where the peoples of the whole world are in view, it is rendered “nations.” The picture draws on Isaiah 60, where nations and kings come to Jerusalem's light bringing their wealth.

verse.text: Its gates will never be shut by day, for there will be no night there,
and they will bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it.
But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or deals in lies, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
Then he showed me a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing out from the throne of God and of the Lamb

down the middle of the city’s main street. On either side of the river was the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.

note.term: down the middle of the city’s main street
note.traditional: In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life

verse.note: The Greek can be punctuated two ways. Read with verse 1, as here and in the edition translated, the river flows down the middle of the street. Read with what follows, as in the King James Version, the tree of life stands in the middle of the street as well as beside the river. The Greek says ‘its street’, meaning the city described in chapter 21.

The image recalls the tree of life in the garden of Genesis 2–3, from which humanity was barred, and Ezekiel 47:12, where trees line both banks of a river flowing from the temple. The Greek noun is singular although it stands on both sides of the river; it may be meant collectively, as a kind of tree.

The Greek says simply ‘twelve fruits’. Many translations take this as twelve varieties; the following clause, ‘yielding its fruit each month’, suggests twelve harvests a year, which is the reading adopted here. Either is possible.
This is the same Greek word that this translation renders ‘Gentiles’ where the non-Jewish peoples are meant. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so ‘nations’ is used.

verse.text: No longer will there be anything under a curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his slaves will serve him;
verse.note: The word is rare and can mean either a curse or a thing placed under one. The sentence echoes Zechariah 14:11, where the underlying idea is the ban that devoted a city to destruction. The promise is that nothing in the new Jerusalem will ever again fall under it.

The word meant a slave, someone owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. Most English versions soften it to ‘servants’, partly because the Septuagint uses it as an honourable title for those who belong to God, such as Moses and the prophets. That honorific sense is present here, but it works through the image of belonging wholly to a master, not instead of it.

verse.text: they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.
And there will be no more night. They have no need of the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.
Then he said to me, “These words are faithful and true. The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his slaves what must happen soon.”

note.traditional: things which must shortly be done

verse.note: The phrase can mean ‘soon’ or ‘swiftly’, that is, without delay once it begins. Most translations take it as ‘soon’, as here. The related adverb in verses 7, 12 and 20 (‘I am coming soon’) has the same ambiguity, and the King James Version has ‘quickly’ there.

text.q: “And look, I am coming soon! Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.”

verse.note: The angel has been speaking, but ‘I am coming’ can only be Jesus, as verses 12–16 and 20 show. The Greek does not mark the change of speaker. Either the angel delivers Jesus’s words in the first person or Jesus’s own voice breaks in; this translation marks the words as his.

verse.text: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I had heard and seen them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who was showing them to me.
But he said to me, “Don’t do that! I am a fellow slave with you and your brothers the prophets and those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!”
Then he said to me, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.

text.q: Let the one who does wrong still do wrong, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do righteousness, and the holy still be holy.”
“Look, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me, to repay each one according to their work.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.
Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by the gates.

verse.note: Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘those who do his commandments’. The two phrases look and sound alike in Greek. The earliest witnesses read ‘wash their robes’, which recalls 7:14, and nearly all modern editions follow them.

text.q: Outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.

verse.note: Dogs in the ancient Mediterranean world were mostly scavengers, and ‘dog’ was a common term of contempt for the unclean or the wicked. Some scholars see a specific reference to male cult prostitutes, as in Deuteronomy 23:18, but this is uncertain.

text.q: I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the assemblies. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.”

verse.note: ‘Church’ is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew the word as the term for a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or institution. The preposition before it is also open: the testimony may be ‘for’, ‘in’ or ‘about’ the assemblies.

verse.text: The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” And let the one who hears say, “Come!” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who wishes take the water of life as a gift.

text.q: “I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to that person the plagues written in this book;

verse.note: The speaker of verses 18–19 is not named. Verse 20 calls Jesus ‘the one who testifies to these things’, so this translation assigns the warning to him, but many interpreters take it as John’s own closing words. The same uncertainty applies to verses 14–15, which may be John’s comment rather than a continuation of Jesus’s speech.

text.q: and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away that person’s share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are written about in this book.”

note.term: share in the tree of life
note.traditional: his part out of the book of life

verse.note: The King James Version reads ‘book of life’, following the first printed Greek text, which at this point depended on the Latin, where ‘book’ and ‘tree’ differ by two letters. Virtually all Greek manuscripts read ‘tree of life’.

verse.text: The one who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!
verse.note: This prayer corresponds to the Aramaic Marana tha, ‘Our Lord, come’, which Paul quotes untranslated in 1 Corinthians 16:22. It appears to have been a fixed prayer of the earliest communities. Here it is the response to Jesus’s promise.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all.
verse.note: The manuscripts differ over the book’s last words: ‘with all’, ‘with the holy ones’, ‘with all the holy ones’ and, in the text behind the King James Version, ‘with you all’. Many add ‘Amen’. The edition translated here prints the shortest form, found in Codex Alexandrinus.
